cards.explanation: The answer is that one man is rich and one is poor. That's how Nathan sets up his story. He's the prophet the LORD sent to David, and he opens with two men in one city and a gap between them you can see from space. No fancy words needed. The text says it right there: “…one rich and the other poor.”

The answer is True. In Nathan's story, the rich man has “…a great number of sheep and cattle…” That man needs a calculator just to count them. Keep that number in your pocket, friends, because it's about to matter. Lots of animals on one side, and only one little lamb on the other.

The answer is daughter. In Nathan's story, the lamb grew up with the poor man and his children, and the text says it was “…like a daughter to him.” Think about that for a second, friends. I think this man loved that little lamb like a member of the family.

The answer is the poor man's lamb. In Nathan's story, the rich man “…refrained from taking one of his own sheep or cattle…” and took the poor man's lamb instead to prepare for his guest. He had a whole herd to pick from and walked right past it. That's like owning a bakery full of cookies and swiping the one your neighbor was saving.

The answer is True. David says, “As surely as the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die!” That's an oath, and he swears it while he's burning with anger. I bet David has no idea how close that sentence is about to land.

The answer is four. David says, “Because he has done this thing and has shown no pity, he must pay for the lamb four times over.” The man's lack of pity is the reason he gives. David's math is strict, and he has no idea whose bill he's writing.

The answer is “You are that man!” Nathan says it to David. David had just said the man in the story deserves to die, and Nathan turns that verdict around on him. Four words, and the story lands right on David. I bet that room went dead quiet.

The answer is True, and listen to the generosity. After listing what He gave, the LORD says to David, “…and if that was not enough, I would have given you even more.” David already had a kingdom, and there was still more on the table. The LORD wasn't running low.

The answer is the Ammonites. The LORD says to David, “You have slain him with the sword of the Ammonites.” The Ammonites were the people Israel was fighting in that war (2 Samuel 11:1). Uriah the Hittite, the husband of Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:3), died in that fighting, and the LORD still says David is the one who slew him. I think this part is heavy.

The answer is that David despised Him and took Uriah's wife. The LORD gives the reason Himself: “…because you have despised Me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your own.” We don't have to guess at it. He names two things, despising Him and taking Uriah's wife. A reason that clear needs no help from me.

The answer is in broad daylight before all Israel. The LORD says to David, “You have acted in secret, but I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel.” Secret on one side, broad daylight on the other. That's about as opposite as it gets. This is a heavy word, and I think David felt every bit of it.
The answer is “I have sinned against the LORD.” David says it plain to Nathan. No excuses, no long speech. He owns it. Nathan answers right away, “The LORD has taken away your sin…”

The answer is False. Nathan tells David, “The LORD has taken away your sin,” and then, “You will not die.” Taken away, and David lives. The consequence that follows is about the son born to him (2 Samuel 12:14), not David himself. The text puts mercy first.

The answer is that he pleads with God and fasts. When David's son is sick, the text says, “David pleaded with God for the boy.” He fasted too, and went into his house for the night. He took it straight to God. I think this is a hard stretch for David.

The answer is False. David stays down. The elders of his household stood beside him to help him up, but he “…would not eat anything with them.” That's how the text puts it. I bet it was hard for them to watch.

The answer is that he might harm himself. The servants say, “He may even harm himself.” They had spoken to David while the child was alive and he wouldn't listen, so they didn't know how he'd take the news. That's a heavy part of the story. I think they were afraid because they cared about him.

The answer is that he sees his servants whispering. The text says, “When David saw that his servants were whispering to one another, he perceived that the child was dead.” He reads the room before anyone says a word. Hushed voices in a quiet house can say plenty. Then he asks them straight out.

The answer is worships. After David got up from the ground, washed and anointed himself, and changed his clothes, he “…went into the house of the LORD and worshiped.” That comes before he asks for any food. The child had just died, and the first place he goes is to the LORD.

The answer is True. After worshiping, David “…went to his own house, and at his request they set food before him, and he ate.” David asks, and they bring it. He had been fasting while the child was alive, so this is a change.

The answer is that he hoped the LORD might let the child live. David gives his own reason: “…‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’” That's hope, resting on the LORD's grace. He fasted and wept because he hoped.

The answer is False. Once the child is dead, David asks, “But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again?” He ends with, “I will go to him, but he will not return to me.” While the child was alive he fasted and wept, and now he lets that go. I think that's a hard thing to say out loud.

The answer is Solomon, David and Bathsheba's son. The text says, “…she gave birth to a son, and they named him Solomon.” It also says, “Now the LORD loved the child”. After a heavy chapter, that's a gentle note to land on.

The answer is because the LORD loved him. The text gives the reason: the LORD “…sent word through Nathan the prophet to name him Jedidiah because the LORD loved him.” The name came with the LORD's love for the boy attached. After all the heavy parts, I think that line is the sweetest one in the chapter. The story of David and Bathsheba ends right here.
